text.title: Two Gallants
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: Two young men, Lenehan and Corley, walk through Dublin on a Sunday evening. Corley arranges to meet a young woman while Lenehan waits, ultimately discovering the outcome of Corley's seduction attempt.

e01-evening-setting.description: The grey warm evening of August descends upon Dublin city, with mild warm air circulating in the streets. The streets are shuttered for Sunday repose but swarmed with a gaily coloured crowd. Lamps shine from tall poles upon the living texture below.

e02-lenehan-corley-introduction.description: Two young men, Lenehan and Corley, come down the hill of Rutland Square. Corley is finishing a long monologue while Lenehan listens with an amused face, walking on the verge of the path.

e03-lenehan-laughs.description: After Corley finishes his narrative, Lenehan laughs noiselessly for fully half a minute and then comments that the story 'takes the biscuit' and is 'recherché'.

e04-lenehan-reputation.description: The narrator reveals Lenehan's reputation as a leech and his survival tactics. He is known for his adroitness and eloquence, his ability to insert himself into groups, and his vast stock of stories, limericks, and riddles. His name is vaguely associated with racing tissues.

e05-corley-asks-where.description: Lenehan asks Corley where he picked up the young woman.

e06-corley-dame-street.description: Corley recounts meeting the young woman under Waterhouse's clock on Dame Street. He describes taking her for a walk by the canal, learning she is a slavey in Baggot Street, and subsequent encounters including visits to Donnybrook where he brought her to a field. He mentions she brought him cigarettes and cigars.

e07-corley-deception.description: Corley reveals his deceptions to Lenehan: he told the girl he was out of a job and working at Pim's, and didn't tell her his real name because he was 'too hairy'. He claims she thinks he is 'a bit of class'.

e08-lenehan-marriage-comment.description: Lenehan suggests that the young woman might think Corley will marry her.

e09-corley-physical-description.description: The narrator describes Corley's physical appearance in detail: he is the son of a police inspector, has inherited his father's frame and gait, walks with hands at his sides holding himself erect, has a large globular oily head that sweats in all weathers, and wears a large round hat set sideways.

e10-corley-social-manner.description: The narrator reveals Corley's social behavior: he is currently about town, relies on friends for job opportunities, is often seen with plainclothes policemen, knows the inner side of affairs, speaks without listening to others, and his conversation is mainly about himself and his reported dialogues.

e11-lenehan-cigarette-offer.description: Lenehan offers his friend Corley a cigarette as the two young men walk through the crowd.

e12-lenehan-moon-observation.description: As they walk, Corley occasionally turns to smile at passing girls, but Lenehan's gaze is fixed on the large faint moon circled with a double halo. He watches earnestly the passing of the grey web of twilight across its face.

e13-lenehan-asks-about-plan.description: Lenehan asks Corley if he supposes he'll be able to 'pull it off all right', referring to the planned seduction.

e14-corley-confident.description: Corley closes one eye expressively as an answer to Lenehan's question, indicating confidence. When Lenehan expresses doubt about whether the girl is 'game for that', Corley assures him she is all right and that he knows how to get around her.

e15-lenehan-lothario-comment.description: Lenehan calls Corley 'a gay Lothario' and 'the proper kind of a Lothario too', with a shade of mockery that relieves the servility of his manner. Lenehan has the habit of leaving his flattery open to the interpretation of raillery.

e16-corley-slavey-preference.description: Corley affirms that there is nothing to touch a good slavey and tells Lenehan to take his tip for it.

e17-corley-past-girls.description: Corley unbosoms himself, recounting how he used to go with girls off the South Circular, taking them out on trams, to bands or plays, or buying them chocolate and sweets. He claims he spent money on them right enough.

e18-corley-past-conquest.description: Corley and Lenehan discuss past romantic experiences. Corley says he got nothing out of his past efforts except from one girl. He moistens his upper lip and gazes at the moon, seeming to meditate. He describes her as 'a bit of all right' with regret.

e19-corley-girl-on-turf.description: Corley reveals that the girl he was fond of is now 'on the turf', having seen her driving down Earl Street one night with two fellows on a car. Lenehan suggests this is Corley's doing, but Corley claims there were others at her before him.

e20-trinity-college-railings.description: As Lenehan and Corley pass along the railings of Trinity College, Lenehan skips out into the road and peers up at the clock.

e21-lenehan-checks-clock.description: Lenehan checks the clock at Trinity College and reports that it is 'Twenty after'.

e22-corley-confident-about-wait.description: Corley says 'Time enough' and assures Lenehan that the girl will be there, adding that he always lets her wait a bit.

e23-harpist-encounter.description: As Lenehan and Corley walk along Nassau Street and turn into Kildare Street, they encounter a harpist standing in the roadway playing to a little ring of listeners. The harpist plays the melody 'Silent, O Moyle' with one hand in the bass and the other in the treble.

e24-stephens-green-arrival.description: The two young men walk up the street without speaking, the mournful music following them. When they reach Stephen's Green they cross the road, where the noise of trams, lights, and crowd release them from their silence.

e25-corley-spots-woman.description: Corley spots the young woman at the corner of Hume Street. She is wearing a blue dress and a white sailor hat, standing on the curbstone and swinging a sunshade in one hand.

e26-lenehan-wants-look.description: Lenehan asks Corley to let him have a look at the young woman.

e27-corley-suspicious.description: Corley glances sideways at his friend and an unpleasant grin appears on his face. He asks if Lenehan is trying to get inside him.

e28-lenehan-insists.description: Lenehan boldly insists he doesn't want an introduction, just a look, and that he's not going to eat her.

e29-corley-agrees.description: Corley becomes more amiable and agrees to the arrangement, saying he'll go over and talk to her while Lenehan passes by.

e30-corley-approaches-woman.description: Corley saunters across the road swaying his head from side to side. He approaches the young woman and, without saluting, begins at once to converse with her. She swings her umbrella more quickly and executes half turns on her heels. Once or twice when he speaks to her at close quarters she laughs and bends her head.

e31-lenehan-observes-woman.description: Lenehan observes them for a few minutes, then walks rapidly along beside the chains and crosses the road obliquely. As he approaches Hume Street corner, he finds the air heavily scented and makes a swift anxious scrutiny of the young woman's appearance. He notes her Sunday finery in detail: blue serge skirt with black leather belt and silver buckle, white blouse, short black jacket with mother-of-pearl buttons, ragged black boa, tulle collarette with disordered ends, and red flowers in her bosom. He notes her stout short muscular body, frank rude health, fat red cheeks, unabashed blue eyes, blunt features, broad nostrils, straggling mouth, and projecting front teeth.

e32-corley-salute.description: As Lenehan passes, he takes off his cap. After about ten seconds, Corley returns a salute to the air by raising his hand vaguely and pensively changing the angle of position of his hat.

e33-lenehan-follows.description: Lenehan walks as far as the Shelbourne Hotel where he halts and waits. After waiting for a little time he sees Corley and the young woman coming towards him. When they turn to the right, he follows them, stepping lightly in his white shoes, down one side of Merrion Square. As he walks on slowly, timing his pace to theirs, he watches Corley's head which turns at every moment towards the young woman's face like a big ball revolving on a pivot.

e34-tram-departure.description: Lenehan keeps the pair in view until he has seen them climbing the stairs of the Donnybrook tram. Then he turns about and goes back the way he came.

e35-lenehan-alone-mood.description: Now that he is alone, Lenehan's face looks older. His gaiety seems to forsake him. As he comes by the railings of the Duke's Lawn, he allows his hand to run along them. The air which the harpist had played begins to control his movements.

e36-lenehan-walks-streets.description: Lenehan walks listlessly round Stephen's Green and then down Grafton Street. Though his eyes take note of many elements of the crowd, they do so morosely. He finds trivial all that was meant to charm him and does not answer the glances which invited him to be bold. He knows he would have to speak a great deal, to invent and to amuse, and his brain and throat are too dry for such a task. The problem of how to pass the hours till he meets Corley again troubles him. He turns to the left when he comes to the corner of Rutland Square and feels more at ease in the dark quiet street.

e37-lenehan-finds-shop.description: Lenehan pauses before the window of a poor-looking shop over which the words 'Refreshment Bar' are printed in white letters. On the glass are two flying inscriptions: 'Ginger Beer' and 'Ginger Ale'. A cut ham is exposed on a great blue dish while near it on a plate lies a segment of very light plum-pudding. He eyes this food earnestly for some time.

e38-lenehan-enters-shop.description: After glancing warily up and down the street, Lenehan goes into the shop quickly. He is hungry, having eaten nothing since breakfast-time except some biscuits which he had asked two grudging curates to bring him. He sits down at an uncovered wooden table opposite two work-girls and a mechanic. A slatternly girl waits on him.

e39-lenehan-orders-food.description: Lenehan asks how much a plate of peas costs. The girl says three halfpence. He orders a plate of peas and a bottle of ginger beer. He speaks roughly in order to belie his air of gentility, as his entry had been followed by a pause of talk.

e40-lenehan-eats.description: The girl brings Lenehan a plate of grocer's hot peas seasoned with pepper and vinegar, a fork, and his ginger beer. He eats his food greedily and finds it so good that he makes a note of the shop mentally. When he has eaten all the peas he sips his ginger beer and sits for some time thinking of Corley's adventure.

e41-lenehan-contemplates.description: In his imagination Lenehan beholds the pair of lovers walking along some dark road. He hears Corley's voice in deep energetic gallantries and sees again the leer of the young woman's mouth. This vision makes him feel keenly his own poverty of purse and spirit. He is tired of knocking about, of pulling the devil by the tail, of shifts and intrigues. He would be thirty-one in November. He wonders if he will ever get a good job or have a home of his own. He thinks how pleasant it would be to have a warm fire to sit by and a good dinner to sit down to. He has walked the streets long enough with friends and with girls. He knows what those friends are worth and knows the girls too. Experience has embittered his heart against the world. But all hope has not left him. He feels better after having eaten, less weary of his life, less vanquished in spirit. He might yet be able to settle down in some snug corner and live happily if he could only come across some good simple-minded girl with a little of the ready.

e42-lenehan-leaves-shop.description: Lenehan pays twopence halfpenny to the slatternly girl and goes out of the shop to begin his wandering again.

e43-lenehan-meets-friends.description: Lenehan goes into Capel Street and walks along towards the City Hall. Then he turns into Dame Street. At the corner of George's Street he meets two friends of his and stops to converse with them. He is glad that he can rest from all his walking. His friends ask him if he has seen Corley and what is the latest. He replies that he has spent the day with Corley. His friends talk very little, looking vacantly after some figures in the crowd and sometimes making a critical remark. One says he has seen Mac an hour before in Westmoreland Street. Lenehan says he has been with Mac the night before in Egan's. The young man who has seen Mac in Westmoreland Street asks if it is true that Mac has won a bit over a billiard match. Lenehan does not know but says that Holohan has stood them drinks in Egan's.

e44-lenehan-at-merrion-street.description: Lenehan leaves his friends at a quarter to ten and goes up George's Street. He turns to the left at the City Markets and walks on into Grafton Street. The crowd of girls and young men has thinned and on his way up the street he hears many groups and couples bidding one another good-night. He goes as far as the clock of the College of Surgeons: it is on the stroke of ten. He sets off briskly along the northern side of the Green hurrying for fear Corley should return too soon. When he reaches the corner of Merrion Street he takes his stand in the shadow of a lamp.

e45-lenehan-waits.description: Lenehan brings out one of the cigarettes which he has reserved and lights it. He leans against the lamp-post and keeps his gaze fixed on the part from which he expects to see Corley and the young woman return.

e46-lenehan-anxiety.description: Lenehan's mind becomes active again. He wonders if Corley has managed it successfully, if he has asked her yet or if he will leave it to the last. He suffers all the pangs and thrills of his friend's situation as well as those of his own. But the memory of Corley's slowly revolving head calms him somewhat: he is sure Corley will pull it off all right. All at once the idea strikes him that perhaps Corley has seen her home by another way and given him the slip. His eyes search the street: there is no sign of them. Yet it is surely half-an-hour since he has seen the clock of the College of Surgeons. Would Corley do a thing like that? He lights his last cigarette and begins to smoke it nervously. He strains his eyes as each tram stops at the far corner of the square. They must have gone home by another way. The paper of his cigarette breaks and he flings it into the road with a curse.

e47-corley-appears.description: Suddenly Lenehan sees Corley and the young woman coming towards him. He starts with delight and, keeping close to his lamp-post, tries to read the result in their walk. They are walking quickly, the young woman taking quick short steps, while Corley keeps beside her with his long stride. They do not seem to be speaking. An intimation of the result pricks Lenehan like the point of a sharp instrument. He knows Corley will fail; he knows it is no go.

e48-corley-silent.description: Corley and the young woman turn down Baggot Street and Lenehan follows them at once, taking the other footpath. When they stop he stops too. They talk for a few moments and then the young woman goes down the steps into the area of a house. Corley remains standing at the edge of the path, a little distance from the front steps. Some minutes pass. Then the hall-door is opened slowly and cautiously. A woman comes running down the front steps and coughs. Corley turns and goes towards her. His broad figure hides hers from view for a few seconds and then she reappears running up the steps. The door closes on her and Corley begins to walk swiftly towards Stephen's Green.

e49-corley-reveals-coin.description: Lenehan hurries on in the same direction. Some drops of light rain fall. He takes them as a warning and, glancing back towards the house which the young woman had entered to see that he is not observed, he runs eagerly across the road. Anxiety and his swift run make him pant. He calls out 'Hallo, Corley!' Corley turns his head to see who has called him, and then continues walking as before. Lenehan runs after him, settling the waterproof on his shoulders with one hand. He calls out again 'Hallo, Corley!' He comes level with his friend and looks keenly in his face. He can see nothing there. He asks 'Well? Did it come off?' They reach the corner of Ely Place. Still without answering, Corley swerves to the left and goes up the side street. His features are composed in stern calm. Lenehan keeps up with his friend, breathing uneasily. He is baffled and a note of menace pierces through his voice. He asks 'Can't you tell us? Did you try her?' Corley halts at the first lamp and stares grimly before him. Then with a grave gesture he extends a hand towards the light and, smiling, opens it slowly to the gaze of his disciple. A small gold coin shines in the palm.

Formalist Reading: Structure, Style, and.name: Formalist Reading: Structure, Style, and Narrative Technique
Formalist Reading: Structure, Style, and.description: A formalist analysis of 'Two Gallants' focusing on narrative structure, stylistic patterns, symbolic imagery, and the formal mechanics of storytelling. This reading emphasizes how Joyce's technical choices—free indirect discourse, spatial organization, imagery patterns, and narrative perspective—construct meaning independent of biographical or historical context.

theme-parasitism-and-dependency.name: Parasitism and Dependency
theme-parasitism-and-dependency.description: The formal structure reveals a parasitic relationship between Lenehan and Corley, mirrored in Lenehan's dependence on observing Corley's conquest. The narrative technique itself enacts this parasitism through Lenehan's perspective dominating the text.

theme-illusion-and-reality.name: Illusion and Reality
theme-illusion-and-reality.description: The gap between Corley's boastful narrative and the actual outcome; between Lenehan's imaginative fantasies and his lived experience; between appearance and truth. Formally enacted through unreliable narration and the delayed revelation of the gold coin.

theme-temporal-structure-and-waiting.name: Temporal Structure and Waiting
theme-temporal-structure-and-waiting.description: The story's formal organization around waiting, anticipation, and the passage of time. The narrative structure mirrors Lenehan's experience of temporal suspension—the long middle section where time is filled with wandering, eating, and anxiety.

theme-urban-geography-and-narrative-move.name: Urban Geography and Narrative Movement
theme-urban-geography-and-narrative-move.description: Dublin's streets function as a formal organizing principle. The narrative moves through specific locations in a mapped sequence; geography becomes a structural device that organizes plot and reflects psychological states.

sym-moon.name: The Moon
sym-moon.description: A formally recurring image that appears at key moments: first observed by Lenehan with a 'double halo,' later referenced when Corley 'gazes at the moon' in regret. The moon functions as a symbol of distance, melancholy, and the passage of time. Its circularity mirrors the circular structure of the narrative.

currentMeanings.description: Distance and separation between characters and their desires

sym-gold-coin.name: The Gold Coin
sym-gold-coin.description: The formal climax of the narrative. A small object that contains enormous symbolic weight through its delayed revelation. The coin represents the proof of seduction, the tangible outcome of Corley's manipulation, and the object of Lenehan's anxious anticipation. Formally, it is the narrative's final image—a moment of visual revelation that resolves the story's central tension.

currentMeanings.description: Material reward for manipulation and deception
The reduction of human intimacy to economic transaction

sym-harp-music.name: The Harp and 'Silent, O Moyle'
sym-harp-music.description: A formally intrusive element—the mournful melody 'Silent, O Moyle' that interrupts the narrative's forward movement. The harp music functions as a formal device that introduces melancholy and controls Lenehan's emotional state. It appears at a structural midpoint and returns to influence Lenehan's solitary wandering, creating a formal echo.

currentMeanings.description: Intrusion of melancholy into the narrative
Artistic beauty in contrast to sordid human action

sym-lamp-post.name: The Lamp-Post
sym-lamp-post.description: A formally significant location where Lenehan waits and where the final revelation occurs. The lamp-post functions as a fixed point in the narrative's spatial geography and as a symbol of illumination—both literal and metaphorical. It is where truth is revealed 'to the gaze of his disciple.'

currentMeanings.description: Witness to human action and moral ambiguity

symrel-moon-lenehan-melancholy.name: Moon as Mirror of Lenehan's Interiority
symrel-moon-lenehan-melancholy.description: The moon's appearance correlates with Lenehan's emotional states. When he observes it early in the narrative, it reflects his capacity for aesthetic appreciation; when Corley gazes at it in regret, it mirrors his emotional depth. The moon becomes a formal device for externalizing internal states.
symrel-moon-lenehan-melancholy.nature: The moon functions as an objective correlative for Lenehan's melancholic consciousness, allowing the narrative to represent interiority through external imagery rather than explicit psychological narration.
symrel-moon-lenehan-melancholy.interpretation: The moon functions as an objective correlative for Lenehan's melancholic consciousness, allowing the narrative to represent interiority through external imagery rather than explicit psychological narration.

symrel-coin-parasitism.name: Gold Coin as Proof of Parasitic Success
symrel-coin-parasitism.description: The coin represents the formal payoff of Corley's parasitic seduction and, by extension, Lenehan's parasitic observation. The coin's revelation is the narrative's climactic moment, formally confirming what the structure has been building toward.
symrel-coin-parasitism.nature: The coin embodies the theme of parasitism by serving as material proof that human relationships have been reduced to economic transactions. Its revelation is the narrative's formal climax.
symrel-coin-parasitism.interpretation: The coin embodies the theme of parasitism by serving as material proof that human relationships have been reduced to economic transactions. Its revelation is the narrative's formal climax.

symrel-harp-temporal-suspension.name: Harp Music as Formal Interruption of Time
symrel-harp-temporal-suspension.description: The harp's mournful melody interrupts the narrative's forward momentum and returns to control Lenehan's movements during his solitary wandering. Formally, the music creates a structural echo and slows narrative pacing.
symrel-harp-temporal-suspension.nature: The harp functions as a formal device that literalizes temporal suspension—the music 'controls' Lenehan's movements, making him a passive subject of aesthetic experience rather than an active agent.
symrel-harp-temporal-suspension.interpretation: The harp functions as a formal device that literalizes temporal suspension—the music 'controls' Lenehan's movements, making him a passive subject of aesthetic experience rather than an active agent.

symrel-lamp-revelation.name: Lamp-Post as Site of Formal Revelation
symrel-lamp-revelation.description: The lamp-post is where the narrative's central mystery is resolved. Corley 'extends a hand towards the light' to reveal the coin, making the lamp-post the formal locus of truth-telling and visual revelation.
symrel-lamp-revelation.nature: The lamp-post's illumination becomes the formal mechanism for distinguishing illusion from reality. The coin's revelation under the lamp's light is the narrative's final image, a moment of perfect formal clarity.
symrel-lamp-revelation.interpretation: The lamp-post's illumination becomes the formal mechanism for distinguishing illusion from reality. The coin's revelation under the lamp's light is the narrative's final image, a moment of perfect formal clarity.

narrator.name: Third-Person Limited Narrator with Free Indirect Discourse
narrator.description: The narrator maintains a predominantly third-person perspective focused on Lenehan, but employs free indirect discourse to blur the boundary between narrator and character consciousness. The narrator is formally unreliable—presenting Corley's boasts without immediate correction, allowing the reader to discover the truth only through Lenehan's observation and the final revelation. The narrative voice is detached and ironic, maintaining formal distance even while inhabiting Lenehan's perspective.

reader.name: Formal Reader Engaged in Interpretive Construction
reader.description: The formalist reader is positioned as an active interpreter of narrative structure, imagery patterns, and stylistic choices. The reader must piece together meaning from the formal organization of the text—the spatial geography of Dublin, the temporal structure of waiting, the recurring imagery of the moon and light. The reader is invited to notice how form generates meaning: how the narrative's structure mirrors Lenehan's experience of temporal suspension, how the delayed revelation of the coin creates narrative tension, how Dublin's geography organizes the plot.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce as a formal innovator who employs free indirect discourse, spatial organization, and symbolic imagery to construct meaning. The author is understood through his technical choices: the use of Dublin as a structural organizing principle, the employment of free indirect discourse to represent consciousness, the careful placement of symbolic images (moon, harp, coin, lamp), and the formal architecture of the narrative that builds toward a climactic revelation.

e01-evening-setting.note: Establishes the formal setting and atmospheric tone. The grey warm evening becomes a structural frame for the entire narrative. The description of Dublin's streets and crowd establishes the urban geography that will organize the plot.

e02-lenehan-corley-introduction.note: Introduces the two central characters and establishes their formal relationship. Corley's monologue and Lenehan's listening position establish the parasitic dynamic that structures the narrative.

e03-lenehan-laughs.note: Demonstrates Lenehan's verbal facility and his role as audience/observer. His laughter and commentary establish his character through action and speech.

e04-lenehan-reputation.note: Formal character exposition that reveals Lenehan's nature through narrative description. The narrator's detached presentation of Lenehan's parasitism establishes the story's moral ambiguity.

e05-corley-asks-where.note: A brief transitional dialogue that prompts Corley's narrative. Formally minimal but functionally necessary to initiate the exposition of Corley's seduction.

e06-corley-dame-street.note: Corley's extended narrative exposition of his seduction. This event establishes the formal pattern of boastful narration that will be undercut by the final revelation. The specific Dublin locations (Dame Street, canal, Baggot Street, Donnybrook) establish the geographic framework.

e07-corley-deception.note: Formally crucial revelation of Corley's deceptions. This event establishes the theme of illusion vs. reality and sets up the narrative's central irony: Corley's boasts about his manipulation will be proven true, but in a way that diminishes rather than elevates him.

e08-lenehan-marriage-comment.note: Lenehan's skeptical interjection introduces doubt about Corley's claims. Formally, this establishes the reader's uncertainty about the truth of Corley's narrative.

e09-corley-physical-description.note: Detailed physical description that establishes Corley's appearance through formal characterization. The description of his 'large globular oily head' and his inherited police inspector's bearing establish his physical presence and social status.

e10-corley-social-manner.note: Formal exposition of Corley's social behavior and character. The narrator's detached description of his self-centeredness and reliance on friends establishes his parasitic nature, paralleling Lenehan's.

e11-lenehan-cigarette-offer.note: A minor action that demonstrates Lenehan's social performance and his attempt to maintain the friendship through small gestures.

e12-lenehan-moon-observation.note: Formally significant introduction of the moon as a recurring symbol. Lenehan's observation of the moon with its 'double halo' establishes a pattern of aesthetic observation that will return throughout the narrative. This moment introduces the symbolic imagery that structures the story's emotional register.

e13-lenehan-asks-about-plan.note: Lenehan's direct question about whether Corley will 'pull it off' formally introduces the central suspense of the narrative. This event establishes the question that will drive the plot forward.

e14-corley-confident.note: Corley's confident response (closing one eye expressively) establishes his boastful certainty. Formally, this creates a contrast with the later revelation that will undercut or complicate this confidence.

e15-lenehan-lothario-comment.note: Lenehan's mockingly flattering comment establishes the formal pattern of his relationship with Corley: flattery mixed with raillery, servility mixed with mockery. This establishes the parasitic dynamic.

e16-corley-slavey-preference.note: Corley's statement about servant girls establishes his predatory preferences and his reduction of women to objects of conquest.

e17-corley-past-girls.note: Corley's narrative of past romantic experiences establishes a pattern of seduction and expenditure. Formally, this exposition of his past behavior sets up expectations for his current conquest.

e18-corley-past-conquest.note: Corley's regretful meditation on a past conquest introduces emotional depth and melancholy. The moon observation here formally echoes Lenehan's earlier moon observation, creating a symbolic pattern.

e19-corley-girl-on-turf.note: The revelation that Corley's past conquest is now 'on the turf' (a prostitute) introduces moral ambiguity and suggests the consequences of Corley's seductions. Formally, this foreshadows the current conquest's potential fate.

e20-trinity-college-railings.note: A transitional action that moves the narrative through Dublin's geography. Trinity College becomes a formal landmark that organizes the spatial movement of the plot.

e21-lenehan-checks-clock.note: The time check ('Twenty after') formally introduces the temporal structure of waiting that will dominate the second half of the narrative. This event establishes the formal concern with time and timing.

e22-corley-confident-about-wait.note: Corley's assertion that 'Time enough' and that he 'always lets her wait a bit' establishes his manipulative control and his casual cruelty. Formally, this comment about making the woman wait foreshadows Lenehan's own waiting.

e23-harpist-encounter.note: The harpist playing 'Silent, O Moyle' is formally significant as an intrusive symbolic element. The mournful melody introduces melancholy and will later 'control' Lenehan's movements. This event establishes a formal pattern of aesthetic interruption.

e24-stephens-green-arrival.note: The arrival at Stephen's Green marks a transition in the narrative. The noise of trams and crowd 'release them from their silence,' formally marking a shift in the narrative's emotional register.

e25-corley-spots-woman.note: The sighting of the young woman is formally crucial. Her appearance in 'blue dress and white sailor hat' establishes her visual presence and marks the beginning of the central action of the narrative.

e26-lenehan-wants-look.note: Lenehan's request to 'have a look' at the woman establishes his role as observer and his parasitic interest in Corley's conquest.

e27-corley-suspicious.note: Corley's suspicious response and 'unpleasant grin' reveal his possessiveness and his awareness of the woman as an object to be guarded. Formally, this establishes the tension between the two men.

e28-lenehan-insists.note: Lenehan's bold insistence establishes his willingness to push against Corley's boundaries. Formally, this demonstrates the dynamic of their relationship.

e29-corley-agrees.note: Corley's agreement to let Lenehan observe establishes the formal arrangement that will structure the narrative's central action.

e30-corley-approaches-woman.note: Corley's approach to the woman is formally significant as the beginning of the seduction in action. His sauntering gait and immediate conversation establish his manipulative technique.

e31-lenehan-observes-woman.note: Lenehan's detailed observation of the woman is formally crucial. The narrator's exhaustive description of her appearance—her clothing, her body, her features—establishes her as an object of scrutiny. This formal objectification mirrors Corley's seductive objectification.

e32-corley-salute.note: The exchange of salutes between Lenehan and Corley is a formal gesture that marks their separation and the beginning of Lenehan's role as observer.

e33-lenehan-follows.note: Lenehan's pursuit of the couple is formally significant. His following them down Merrion Square, watching Corley's head 'revolving on a pivot,' establishes the formal pattern of observation that structures the narrative.

e34-tram-departure.note: The couple's boarding of the Donnybrook tram marks the formal separation of Lenehan from the central action. This event initiates the long middle section of the narrative where Lenehan waits and wanders.

e35-lenehan-alone-mood.note: Lenehan's mood change when alone is formally significant. The narrator's observation that 'his face looks older' and 'his gaiety seems to forsake him' marks a shift in the narrative's emotional register. The harp music begins to 'control his movements,' establishing the formal pattern of aesthetic influence.

e36-lenehan-walks-streets.note: Lenehan's solitary wandering through Dublin is formally crucial. This extended passage establishes the temporal structure of waiting and the psychological state of anxiety. The narrator's description of his morose observation and his exhaustion establishes the emotional register of the narrative's middle section.

e37-lenehan-finds-shop.note: The discovery of the refreshment bar is formally significant as a moment of visual attention. Lenehan's observation of the food in the window establishes his hunger and his material need.

e38-lenehan-enters-shop.note: Lenehan's entry into the shop marks a formal shift in the narrative. The description of his hunger and his self-conscious performance of roughness establishes his social anxiety and his material precarity.

e39-lenehan-orders-food.note: The food order is formally significant as a moment of economic transaction. Lenehan's rough speech to 'belie his air of gentility' establishes his social performance and his anxiety about class.

e40-lenehan-eats.note: Lenehan's eating is formally significant as a moment of physical satisfaction and mental relief. The narrator notes that he 'feels better after having eaten,' establishing the formal connection between physical and psychological states.

e41-lenehan-contemplates.note: Lenehan's extended contemplation is formally crucial. This long passage of free indirect discourse represents Lenehan's interiority—his fantasies about Corley's conquest, his regrets about his own life, his hopes for future stability. This event is formally significant as the narrative's deepest exploration of Lenehan's consciousness.

e42-lenehan-leaves-shop.note: Lenehan's departure from the shop is a brief transitional moment that marks the end of the shop sequence and the resumption of his wandering.

e43-lenehan-meets-friends.note: The encounter with friends is formally significant as a moment of social performance. Lenehan's conversation with his friends establishes his role as a social participant and his knowledge of Dublin's social networks.

e44-lenehan-at-merrion-street.note: Lenehan's arrival at Merrion Street and his positioning in the lamp's shadow is formally crucial. This event establishes the formal setting for the narrative's climax. The time check ('on the stroke of ten') establishes the temporal structure of waiting.

e45-lenehan-waits.note: Lenehan's waiting at the lamp-post is formally significant as a moment of suspended anticipation. His lighting a cigarette and fixing his gaze establishes the formal pattern of observation.

e46-lenehan-anxiety.note: Lenehan's anxious speculation about whether Corley has 'managed it successfully' is formally crucial. This extended passage of internal monologue represents the narrative's peak of suspense and anxiety. The formal representation of his uncertainty and his eventual conviction that Corley will succeed establishes the psychological tension.

e47-corley-appears.note: Corley's appearance with the young woman is formally crucial. Lenehan's intuition that 'he knows Corley will fail' based on their walk marks a formal reversal of expectation. This event initiates the narrative's final movement toward revelation.

e48-corley-silent.note: The silent walk down Baggot Street and the mysterious encounter at the house is formally significant. The appearance of the woman running down the steps and the cryptic exchange with Corley establishes the ambiguity that will be resolved by the coin's revelation.

e49-corley-reveals-coin.note: The revelation of the gold coin is the narrative's formal climax. This event is maximally significant as the moment where all the narrative's tension is resolved. The formal description of Corley extending his hand 'towards the light' and opening it 'slowly to the gaze of his disciple' makes this moment the narrative's final image and its ultimate revelation of truth.

lenehan.note: Lenehan is the formal center of the narrative. The story is structured around his perspective, his observations, his waiting, and his interiority. He is the primary consciousness through which the narrative is filtered.

corley.note: Corley is formally significant as the object of Lenehan's observation and as the agent of the central action (the seduction). His boasts and his final revelation structure the narrative's central tension.

young-woman.note: The young woman is formally significant as the object of both Corley's seduction and Lenehan's observation. Her detailed physical description establishes her as a formal object of scrutiny. She remains largely silent and passive, existing primarily as an object of male desire and manipulation.

harpist.note: The harpist is formally significant as the source of the mournful melody that intrudes into the narrative and influences Lenehan's emotional state. The harpist represents aesthetic interruption and formal control of atmosphere.

slatternly-girl.note: The waitress is formally significant as a minor character who serves Lenehan and witnesses his social performance. She represents the working-class service economy.

mechanic.note: The mechanic is a minor background figure in the refreshment bar scene.

work-girls.note: The work-girls are minor background figures in the refreshment bar scene.

two-friends.note: Lenehan's friends are formally significant as representatives of his social network and as witnesses to his social performance. Their vacuous conversation establishes the emptiness of Dublin's social world.

mac.note: Mac is mentioned only in conversation and serves as a reference point for Dublin's social networks.

holohan.note: Holohan is mentioned only in conversation as someone who has stood drinks.

dairyman.note: The dairyman is mentioned by Corley as a previous acquaintance of the young woman, establishing her history of relationships.

old-fellow.note: The old fellow is mentioned as a source of cigars, establishing the young woman's previous relationships and her role in obtaining gifts.

corley-father.note: Corley's father (the police inspector) is mentioned as the source of Corley's inherited bearing and social status. He represents paternal authority and institutional power.

woman-in-house.note: The mysterious woman who runs down the steps is formally significant as an ambiguous figure whose identity and relationship to the young woman remains unclear. She represents the narrative's final mystery.

dublin-city.note: Dublin itself is formally significant as the organizing principle of the narrative. The city's streets, landmarks, and geography structure the plot and establish the spatial framework within which the action unfolds.

abs-corley-seduction-success.note: The success or failure of Corley's seduction is the central formal tension of the narrative. The entire structure of the story is organized around the question of whether Corley will 'pull it off.' The gold coin's revelation confirms his success, making this absential the narrative's central concern.

abs-lenehan-social-belonging.note: Lenehan's desire to belong to social groups is formally significant as a driving force in his character. His parasitic behavior and his observation of Corley are motivated by his need for social connection and his anxiety about exclusion.

abs-lenehan-material-comfort.note: Lenehan's longing for material comfort (a home, a good job, a warm fire) is formally significant as the content of his extended contemplation in the refreshment bar. This absential represents his unfulfilled desires and his material precarity.

abs-young-woman-marriage.note: The young woman's possible expectation of marriage is formally significant as an unspoken assumption that structures the seduction. Lenehan's comment about marriage introduces this absential, and it remains unresolved throughout the narrative.

abs-lenehan-fear-of-failure.note: Lenehan's fear that he will never escape his poverty and parasitic existence is formally significant as the emotional subtext of his contemplation and his anxious waiting. This absential represents the narrative's underlying melancholy.
